docs.excerpt: Small language models that run on your own machine (via Ollama, or fully in-browser via WebAssembly).
docs.text: Local Models Small language models that run on your own machine (via Ollama, or fully in browser via WebAssembly). They are less capable than frontier cloud models but keep your data private, cost nothing per call, and work offline. Reckons.AI uses them where they score well: chat, diff summaries, and merge analysis can prefer a reachable local model automatically, while harder extraction stays with your chosen backend. In this section Structured Outputs Instead of asking a model for free form text and hoping it is parseable, structured output constrains generation to a fixed schema (specific fields, specific types). docs.title: Models Are Tools, Not Thinkers
docs.excerpt: A language model is a tool -- powerful, but still a tool.
docs.text: Models Are Tools, Not Thinkers A language model is a tool powerful, but still a tool. It cannot verify its own outputs, does not know what is true, and will confidently produce plausible sounding falsehoods. Calling them 'AI' implies agency they do not have. Treat them as highly capable text prediction engines.

docs.title: Structured Outputs
docs.excerpt: Instead of asking a model for free-form text and hoping it is parseable, structured output constrains generation to a fixed schema (specific fields, specific types).
docs.text: Structured Outputs Instead of asking a model for free form text and hoping it is parseable, structured output constrains generation to a fixed schema (specific fields, specific types). This matters most for small local models: a 1 4B parameter model frequently produces broken free form JSON but stays reliable when the schema is enforced. Reckons.AI uses schema constrained extraction so local models can turn text into clean facts which still land as pending for your review.

docs.title: What Language Models Actually Are
docs.excerpt: The models people call 'AI' are trained statistical models built with human knowledge at every level.
docs.text: What Language Models Actually Are The models people call 'AI' are trained statistical models built with human knowledge at every level. Humans wrote the training data, designed the architecture, labeled the fine tuning examples, and aligned the outputs. These models predict likely text based on patterns they do not think, reason, or understand. In this section Built on Human Knowledge Every layer of a language model relies on human work. The training corpus is human written text. The architecture was designed by human researchers. RLHF alignment uses human judgments. The model's outputs are a reflection of collective human knowledge, filtered through statistical compression. Graph Grounded Accuracy When an LLM has access to your reviewed knowledge graph, its outputs become dramatically more accurate. Hallucination When a model generates plausible sounding but false information. This is not a bug it is an inherent property of how text prediction works. The model optimizes for likelihood, not truth. This is exactly why human review matters. Local Models Small language models that run on your own machine (via Ollama, or fully in browser via WebAssembly). Models Are Tools, Not Thinkers A language model is a tool powerful, but still a tool. Prompt Engineering The art of structuring input to get useful output from a language model. A Reckoning is a structured prompt: Situation + Target + your graph context. The better the input, the better the output. Related Graph Grounded Accuracy What Language Models Actually Are

docs.title: The thesis
headings: An unverifiable claim, made by the party it benefits, is not evidence.
We would rather show you no citation than a forged one.
The most useful thing a graph can hold is a well-formed absence.
A forced link is worse than an orphan.
Export is a right. Distribution is a privilege.
A private graph makes no claim on anybody.
We will not describe a control we do not have.
No account until an account is unavoidable.
Knowing something should not require permission.
docs.text: The thesis Most knowledge tools store what you know. Reckons.AI stores HOW YOU KNOW IT — and refuses to fake it when it cannot. The tenets An unverifiable claim, made by the party it benefits, is not evidence. What we believe — a commitment, not a control. Nothing enforces this. This is the spine. We arrived at it three separate times from three different directions: a stated purpose does not unlock a content gate, a weak similarity does not justify a link, and a source you control yourself is not a source. Each time the answer was the same — so we stopped treating it as a rule and started treating it as the thesis. We would rather show you no citation than a forged one. Enforced in code — there is a mechanism, and it runs. Every extracted fact quotes the sentence it came from — and we CHECK that the quote is really in your source. Language models paraphrase, and a paraphrased citation is a forgery that looks right. If we cannot find the quote, we drop it and lower our confidence. A missing receipt is honest. A convincing fake is not. The most useful thing a graph can hold is a well formed absence. Enforced in code — there is a mechanism, and it runs. You cannot ask a question you have not discovered you have. So a fact whose object is still unknown is not a gap in the graph — it is the point of it. Subject known, predicate known, object still open, and four things stalled behind it. That turns 'go find out what we are missing' into 'answer this one question'. The knowledge you need to decide is usually a few people away; the hard part was never reaching them, it was knowing what to ask. A forced link is worse than an orphan. What we believe — a commitment, not a control. Nothing enforces this. Disconnected facts are merely less useful. An invented edge is a lie the graph tells itself — it LOOKS like knowledge and is not. So if a new fact does not genuinely connect to what you already know, we connect it to nothing and say so. 'Is related to' is a non link wearing the costume of a link. Export is a right. Distribution is a privilege. Enforced in code — there is a mechanism, and it runs. Your graph is a plain text file on your machine, and we will never withhold it from you — whatever it contains. But when WE are the one carrying your content to someone else, we are a participant in that delivery, and we take responsibility for what we carry. We gate only what we carry. A private graph makes no claim on anybody. Enforced in code — there is a mechanism, and it runs. Think privately. Be wrong privately. Change your mind privately. Your own graph needs no permission, no account, and no provenance — because it makes no claim on anyone else. Provenance is a claim made TO SOMEONE; alone with your notes, there is nobody to substantiate it to, and no reason to pretend otherwise. We will not describe a control we do not have. Enforced in code — there is a mechanism, and it runs. Our safety documentation states plainly which protections exist and which do not, and an automated check verifies them against the live code every week — recording the failures too. We have already caught ourselves overclaiming, and corrected it in public. A safety promise you cannot verify is just marketing. No account until an account is unavoidable. Enforced in code — there is a mechanism, and it runs. There is no sign up, no email, and no server holding your graph — the app is static files and a browser database, so there is nothing to log in TO. Where a feature genuinely cannot work without an account, it is YOUR account with a service you chose: your API key, your n8n, your Cloudflare. Publishing and cross device sync are where this will be tested, and neither is solved yet. Open source wins the tie. Enforced in code — there is a mechanism, and it runs. The application is MIT licensed and your graph is stored in Turtle, a W3C standard rather than a private format with an exporter bolted on. If we disappeared tomorrow, your graph and the code that reads it would both still work. The honest part: the strongest models this app can call are not open, and a local one is measurably worse at extraction today. Knowing something should not require permission. What we believe — a commitment, not a control. Nothing enforces this. Enclosing knowledge behind a login, a subscription, or a format one vendor controls is a choice somebody made, not a property of the knowledge. The tools for thinking with what you know should be free to use, read, and leave. This is a BELIEF, not a control — nothing in the code enforces it, and it is why the other tenets are shaped the way they are.

docs.text: Contributing How this repository is developed and tested — for people changing the code, not using the app. Coding workflow Agent orchestration — bring your own harness (PLANNED, not built) THIS DOES NOT EXIST YET. The design: a task is a triple — goal, tier, harness preference, due at, blocked by, outcome — and any harness can drain the queue: Claude Code, Codex, a local Ollama script, or a human in the review queue. The graph becomes the orchestration config, so the queue outlives whichever agent CLI is fashionable this quarter, and a harness that hits a usage limit hands its task back rather than stalling it forever. Agents ask the graph, not you When an agent needs a decision it cannot make, it does not stop and wait for you. It emits the question AS A PARTIAL FACT into the graph — subject and predicate known, object '?', plus a note on what the question blocks — and moves to the next unblocked task. You answer whenever you like, in the review queue. The answer flows back and the waiting work resumes. Check your work against the plan (git analysis) The graph knows what you INTENDED. Git knows what you DID. Git analysis compares them: kb check plan tells you whether the work you are about to do matches something planned; kb git diff triples finds which graph entities your diff actually touched; kb alignment score gives a 0 1 score across four dimensions (coverage, status alignment, dependency respect, scope discipline). Commits that match no planned work are flagged as unplanned — not blocked, but not invisible either. CI/CD graph watch — the plan reviews your PR On every push and pull request, CI compares the code changes against the plan in the graph and posts an alignment report as a PR comment: score, discrepancies, drift warnings, and a KB snapshot artifact. Drift is surfaced where the review already happens, rather than in a dashboard nobody opens. Coding workflow Reckons.AI turns a codebase into a graph you can interrogate, and then keeps the code and the plan honest with each other. The plan lives in the graph; code is checked against it; agents propose, humans decide. This page is generated from that same graph, so it cannot claim a capability the graph does not have. Consistency comes from YOUR context, not from a better model The facts that did the work in that session were not general knowledge, and no model would have produced them from training. 'Granularity breeds rubber stamping — a review list that is too fine trains the human to accept all.' 'Cleaning is itself damaging; an automated tidy up that drops a fact you needed is worse than the mess.' 'Spend attention on disagreement, not agreement.' 'Unclassified fails toward the human.' These are one person's judgments, formed on this project, written down once. Because they were in the graph, they constrained work months later — an accept all control shipped WITH outlier highlighting rather than without it, because the graph objected. Feed an agent the graph, not the repo kb compress selects the relevant subgraph for a question and serializes it compactly, so an agent gets grounded context instead of a directory listing. Ingest a repository into a graph Point Reckons.AI at a repository and it builds a Codebase graph: modules, their source files (kpred:has file), and the relationships between them. The result is queryable — 'which module owns this file', 'what does this depend on' — instead of grep and hope. One report that grows, instead of twenty that interrupt Agents append findings — bug found, claim falsified, shipped, decision needed — to a single dated digest while you are away, and each finding is also written into the graph as a pending fact on the entity it concerns. You come back to one accumulating page, not a scrollback to reconstruct. One session, five features not rebuilt Five requests arrived across a single session on 2026 07 19, each framed as new work — and every one of them had already been decided months earlier. The agent had no memory of those sessions; the graph did: (1) 'summarize a node and its relations' was the unbuilt remainder of F65 entity sets, F96 quick graph settings and the graph legibility condensation idea; (2) 'group review triples and accept a set' was loop job grouping, which already specified batch accept with outlier highlighting — only the topical relevance axis was genuinely new; (3) 'graphs need HNSW style jumps to sub graphs' met hierarchy nav (layers within a graph) and KBLeap (jumps between graphs), narrowing the work to the one missing middle rung; (4) 'find the most relevant graph for this ingest' met routeQuestion(), already built and tested, needing only a generalized input; (5) the AI council merge met loop subagent graphs, which had already established that a sub agent returns a graph and that merging graphs is the product. Task scheduling in the graph (PLANNED, not built) THIS DOES NOT EXIST YET. Tasks, schedules and outcomes as graph facts, drained by whichever runner is available — the in app worker on any device, an optional desktop process, or the MCP server when an agent is already connected. The local agent tier — a first pass that never touches your source A local model (via Ollama, on your own hardware) reviews a diff, drafts a missing description, or reads for staleness — always inside a scripted harness: ground it in the graph, constrain the prompt, validate the output, emit a PROPOSAL. It writes to the review queue. It never writes to source, and it never writes to the graph. The saving is not compression — it is the feature you did not build twice The usual pitch for a knowledge graph in front of a coding agent is token compression: feed a dense subgraph instead of re reading the repo. That saving is real but modest. The larger one is structural — an agent that can query what you already decided proposes an EXTENSION to an existing feature instead of a new feature under a slightly different name. A duplicate feature is not a one off cost: you pay to build it, then pay forever to maintain two things that should have been one, and the second one drifts from the first the first time either is tuned. The script tier — checks that cannot hallucinate Deterministic checks that run on every push and cost nothing: graph invariants (dead file links, invalid statuses, duplicate IDs, dangling dependencies); evidence for status claims (a feature marked shipped must link a test or declare that it has none — you may ship untested code, but not silently); prompt/safety preamble drift; production build verification; and a license gate on every third party dependency we study. Work tiering — stop paying frontier prices for rules Every recurring task is routed to the cheapest tier that can do it correctly. SCRIPT: the answer is checkable by a rule ('does this path exist', 'is this status in the enum') — deterministic code, zero tokens, zero hallucination, runs in CI. LOCAL AGENT: the answer is judgment over language and being wrong is cheap, because the output is a proposal a human gates — a local model inside a scripted harness that grounds it, validates its output, and emits a reviewable proposal. FRONTIER: cross file architectural reasoning, deciding process, and code that lands. Testing Graph Management Page The /kb page showing the graph registry, predicate manager, and workspace controls. Ingest Page The /ingest page with text, URL, file, and graph import tabs. Verified for correct tab rendering and input field visibility. Main Page (Empty graph) The graph view with an empty knowledge graph. Should show the empty state message and Shelly greeting, not a blank screen. Main Page (Mobile) Main graph view on mobile viewport (375x812). NavBar collapses to hamburger, graph fills screen, touch targets are 44px minimum. Main Page (Tablet) Main graph view on tablet viewport (768x1024). Intermediate layout between mobile and desktop. Page Screenshots Baseline visual regression screenshots for each major page. These are not stories but single page captures used for pixel analysis and DOM overlap detection. Reckons.AI Graph Review — Goal & Workflow The Reckons.AI Graph Review is an offline, exhaustive audit of the whole app treated as a graph: every button is clicked, every screen is visually checked, and every finding is tied back to the graph for human review. It runs locally and Opus reviewed — no cloud dependency — and scores against the Web/Mobile UI UX rubric. The goal Catch the failures a "click everything, flag crashes" pass misses — silent no ops (a control that fires, throws nothing, and does nothing) and stale cache regressions — while producing a reviewable, graph native record rather than a throwaway log. Workflow overview 1. Enumerate — collect every interactive element on every route (buttons, tabs, leap badges, sheets). 2. Act and assert a delta — click each, then check that something observable actually changed (URL, node count, graph id, open panels, title, visible text). This is what catches silent no ops. 3. Visual check — pixel, DOM overlap and touch target checks run locally; a local VLM scores each screenshot against the rubric. 4. docs.title: How this site is built
docs.excerpt: This documentation site is generated from the graph that describes Reckons.AI — including the parts that are still wrong.
docs.text: How this site is built This site is not written. It is composed — from the same knowledge graph that describes Reckons.AI to itself. This page explains how, and is honest about what does not work yet. It is also the one page here that is genuinely hand written. That is deliberate, and the reason is explained at the bottom. The problem this solves Until recently /docs published one page per entity . Any subject in the documentation graphs carrying a type became its own file, which produced 269 pages sorted alphabetically with no editorial layer. The sidebar was 23,000 pixels tall and held 815 links. Real documentation sat beside internal bookkeeping like "GUIDE.md → Superseded" — a note about this repository's own file migration, published as public documentation. Nothing had gone wrong mechanically. The generator did exactly what it was told. The mistake was in what it was told: "has a type" was standing in for "is a page someone would want to read" , so the graph was deciding the site's information architecture by accident. Three graphs, not one The site is described by three graphs with different jobs. The design graph ( static/website.ttl ) says what the site should be. Eight pages, each declaring which datasets it draws on and — required, not optional — why a reader would open it . A page with no stated purpose is refused at build time, because a page nobody can state the point of is precisely what the 269 already were. It uses standard vocabulary rather than invented terms: schema:WebPage for pages, schema:isBasedOn for the source relation, schema:abstract for purpose, void:Dataset for each source graph, and dcat:Catalog to hold the set together. The status graph ( static/website status.ttl ) says what the site actually is . It is generated by walking the published files and reading each one through the same parser the site uses. Crucially it is derived from the output , never written alongside it — a status graph produced from the same source as the pages would agree with itself by construction and prove nothing. The archive is git, for now. That is a deliberate choice rather than a gap: for text under version control, a parallel journal would duplicate what git already does well. Composition Each page declares its sources, and composition gathers the matching entities into it, grouped by which graph each part came from. One page can draw on several graphs — How it works composes both the architecture and the triples and RDF datasets, and says which section came from which. The safeguard matters more than the feature: composition refuses to run if any entity would be left unclaimed. Reducing 269 pages to 8 is an editorial act, and the difference between curated and we lost 250 pages of content is entirely whether the leftovers are visible. Run npm run docs:consolidate and it reports exactly what every page covers and what nothing covers. Some entities are deliberately excluded , and an exclusion is not the same as an oversight. The markdown migration tracker — those 22 "→ Superseded" entries — is excluded by a rule that carries its reason. An exclusion without a stated reason is refused. Cross links are derived, not written Entities relate to each other in the graph. When consolidation moved them onto shared pages those relationships did not disappear — they became invisible. So the generator reads them back and emits a See also line pointing at whichever page now holds the related entity. Nobody maintains those links. They are recomputed on every build, and they cannot rot into pointing at a page that no longer exists. The site measures itself npm run website:align This compares the design graph against the observed status graph and scores the gap. It keeps four kinds of divergence separate, because they need different responses: Undeclared — published, but the design never asked for it. Wants a decision. Unbuilt — designed, but does not exist. Wants building. Divergent — exists in both, and they disagree. The only unambiguous bug. Aligned — agreement. When this consolidation began the score was 0% : 271 pages the design did not describe and 8 designed pages that did not exist. "The docs are a mess" is true and unactionable; 0% aligned, 271 undeclared is the same statement in a form you can work to zero. What is not built Stating this plainly is a house rule here — a plan written in the present tense is a lie with good manners. The status graph observes files, not rendering. It knows a page exists and what it claims to be. It cannot tell you what a browser actually painted, so a page can appear correct and render broken. The graph records those blind spots explicitly rather than leaving them implied. Section variety. Every composed section renders the same way — a heading and a definition. Cards, callouts and richer layouts are not expressible in the design graph yet. Links into the graph view. A page cannot yet link a reader to the interactive graph its content came from. The deep link does not exist: the app's ?kb= parameter names a local database, not one of these published graphs. Design intent is only partly checked. The graph declares things like disclosure style, and nothing yet verifies the rendered page honours them. Why this page is hand written Every other page here is generated, and editing one directly would be pointless — the next build overwrites it. This page carries no source declaration, which is what marks it hand authored. The generator skips it entirely, the alignment report still counts it, and it is safe to edit by hand or through the CMS. That distinction is the seam the site is being refined through: generated pages are changed by editing the graph; pages like this one are changed by writing. The harder question is what happens when someone edits a generated page to add their own voice. Today the answer is that the next regeneration overwrites it. That is a known limitation with a plan behind it, not a decision anyone is happy with.

docs.title: Reckons.AI v0.1.0
docs.excerpt: The first tagged release: local-first knowledge graphs, multi-provider LLM extraction, 2D/3D graph views, Shelly, a browser extension, an MCP server, cross-KB alignment, and graph-published docs.
docs.text: Reckons.AI v0.1.0 The first tagged release of Reckons.AI, a local first personal knowledge graph that runs entirely in your browser. Here is an honest summary of what shipped. Highlights Local first knowledge graphs — Statements live in IndexedDB (via Dexie); no server is required. Each graph is a portable, versionable store you can export as Turtle at any time. Multi provider LLM extraction with review — Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama, OpenRouter, Chrome's built in AI, or a fully offline WASM model extract facts from whatever you ingest. Every extracted statement lands in a review workflow (pending, confirmed, refined, rejected, superseded) before it is trusted. 2D and 3D graph views — Explore your knowledge as an interactive force directed graph, with per entity icons, hierarchy layouts, and 3D models for key nodes. Shelly, the in app assistant — A chat companion that can search, explain, and tour your graph, including guided stories with text to speech playback. Browser extension — Capture pages as you browse, accumulate a research session across tabs, and batch ingest with at a glance conflict and reinforcement summaries. MCP server — Query your knowledge graphs from Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or any MCP client: full text search, subgraph traversal, AI grounded reckonings (situation to target to proposal), and git aware alignment checks against a project's own roadmap. Cross KB alignment — Compare and merge entities across two graphs, with embedding based matching and IRI remapping for the parts you accept. Graph published docs — This documentation site is generated from a Reckons.AI graph and published through a Sveltia CMS backed workflow: pages are graph nodes, markdown is a generated by product, and a CI check keeps the two in sync. Under the hood A content safety preamble is injected into every LLM call, backed by a pattern based classifier that filters disallowed content before it ever reaches your graph. BGE small en v1.5 embeddings power semantic search, merge detection, and cross KB entity matching. The product's own roadmap, architecture, and test coverage are documented as queryable TTL knowledge bases rather than scattered markdown files, with a git aware alignment check to catch drift between code and plan. What's next Progressive enrichment pipelines, a VS Code integration, and enterprise access controls are on the roadmap. See the Docs for what has shipped and what is still planned.

docs.title: Reckons.AI v0.2.0
docs.excerpt: The first release since v0.1.0: currents, archive, publishing, a deterministic offline tier — and a run of fixes for features that were green in tests and dead in a browser.
headings: Fixes that matter more than they look
docs.text: Reckons.AI v0.2.0 454 commits since v0.1.0, 157 of them features. This is the honest summary — what shipped, and what is still not true. Highlights Currents — sources you subscribe to, arriving as translucent pod view nodes for review rather than landing silently in the graph. Archive — sweep old facts into a dated archive graph, with a journal that can be rewound. An ingest that mentions an archived entity now offers to restore it instead of quietly minting a duplicate. Graph publishing — WebPage nodes round trip to content/ .md , so this page and the rest of the docs are composed from the graph rather than written beside it. A deterministic offline tier — 19 checks that cost nothing to run: graph invariants, SHACL shapes, CSP origins, claim auditing, safety attestation. They run before every PR and are the reason several of the fixes below were found at all. Multi graph work — cross graph alignment, KB leaps, graph sets, and duplicate detection that can now compare copies rather than only reporting them. Fixes that matter more than they look A theme ran through this release: features that were green in tests and dead in a browser . Repo ingest and site export had never worked from a browser. api.github.com was missing from the Content Security Policy allowlist since the initial release commit, so the browser refused the request before sending it. Both were marked shipped. Also fixed for Tavily, Firecrawl, and the default Reckons provider URL — and a script now checks every fetched origin against the policy, so this class cannot return quietly. Self hosted Indico could never be reached , for the same reason plus missing CORS. The verifier was 6/6 green because it ran in Node, where neither is enforced. The timeline placed undated nodes at their ingestion time , so 93% of the starter graph sat in a wall at "today" and compressed the real events into a tenth of the axis. Undated nodes now get their own labelled lane. Imported events were two hours wrong — Indico renders times in the category's timezone, which the mapper discarded. Safety The ethics preamble is no longer injected into every prompt. It is gated by purpose and locality : anything shared always carries it, remote conversation carries it, and local only or structured output paths do not — the latter because every written statement already passes a deterministic content classifier regardless of what a model was told. The ordering is now tested: a custom persona cannot precede the preamble, and a shared persona served from a local model still carries it. What is still not true The review queue holds 736 proposals and none has ever been ruled on . There is now a metric that says so. Estimates exist on five designs and only two have been scored; both came in under. SHACL validation reports and does not gate — nothing in the app is blocked by a shape yet, and users cannot author shapes for their own graphs. staging had drifted 84 commits behind main ; this release reconciles the pipeline. Seventeen js/file system race findings are open, not the seven an earlier draft of this page claimed — that number came from a partial query and was wrong. Sixteen already existed on main ; this release adds the same pattern in two new scripts. Every one is a check then act on a file ( if (!existsSync(p)) writeFileSync(p, …) ) in build and agent scripts — none of it ships in the app bundle. They are known, unfixed, and deliberately not bundled into this release; the fix is its own branch because it is mechanical and touches twelve files.

docs.excerpt: A W3C standard for representing knowledge as a graph of linked statements.
docs.text: RDF (Resource Description Framework) A W3C standard for representing knowledge as a graph of linked statements. The foundation of the Semantic Web. RDF itself is abstract Turtle, JSON LD, and RDF/XML are concrete serialization formats. In this section JSON LD JSON based serialization for RDF. Embeds linked data in standard JSON using a @context object. Popular for web APIs. Linked Data Tim Berners Lee's principles for publishing data on the web: use IRIs, use HTTP, provide useful RDF, and link to other datasets. PROV O (Provenance Ontology) A W3C vocabulary for expressing provenance: who created something, when, and from what sources. Reckons.AI uses prov:wasDerivedFrom to link statements to their source. RDF Schema (RDFS) A vocabulary for describing classes and properties: rdfs:Class, rdfs:subClassOf, rdfs:domain, rdfs:range, rdfs:label, rdfs:comment. Reckons.AI uses rdfs:label for human readable entity names. SKOS (Simple Knowledge Organization System) A vocabulary for taxonomies and concept hierarchies using skos:broader, skos:narrower, skos:related. This documentation file uses SKOS to organize concepts. SPARQL The query language for RDF graphs. Like SQL for relational databases, but for triple stores. Example: SELECT ?name WHERE {String.fromCharCode(123)} ?person foaf:name ?name {String.fromCharCode(125)}

docs.excerpt: The fundamental unit of knowledge in RDF: a three-part statement -- subject, predicate, object.
docs.text: The Semantic Triple The fundamental unit of knowledge in RDF: a three part statement subject, predicate, object. Any fact expressible in human language can be expressed as a triple. Triples connect to form a graph, and graphs reveal relationships that documents hide. In this section IRI (Identifier) A globally unique identifier for a resource. IRIs are the names of things in RDF like URLs but for any concept, not just web pages. Example: urn:reckons:guide/WhatIsReckonsAI Knowledge Graph A graph structured database where entities are nodes and relationships are edges. Multiple triples form a graph. The same subject can appear in many triples, creating a web of connected knowledge. A graph is nodes and the named edges between them. Rendered once at build time, so this page still ships no JavaScript. A graph is nodes and the named edges between them. Rendered once at build time, so this page still ships no JavaScript. Why it is this way Note Reckons.AI renders your knowledge graph as an interactive 3D force directed graph. Detail Scene Height 480 Scene Width 1200 Literal Values A data value in RDF: a string, number, date, or boolean. Literals can have a language tag (@en) or a datatype IRI (^^xsd:integer). Example: '42'^^xsd:integer is a typed literal. Plain Text Portability Your knowledge graph exports as a .ttl file plain text, human readable, no proprietary format. Provenance Every triple in Reckons.AI carries its source. You always know where a fact came from, how trusted that source is, and when it was added. Metadata about metadata this is what makes a graph trustworthy. RDF (Resource Description Framework) A W3C standard for representing knowledge as a graph of linked statements. Reification Making a statement about a statement. In RDF, reification assigns an IRI to a triple so it can be annotated with provenance, confidence, or temporal bounds. Reckons.AI uses reification in its TTL export format. Subject Predicate Object Subject: the entity being described (always an IRI). Predicate: the relationship or property (always an IRI). Object: the value or target (an IRI or a literal string/number/date). Example: 'Alice worksAt AcmeCorp'. Example: 'Policy covers water damage'. What we found Example In 'Earth orbits Sun', Earth=subject, orbits=predicate, Sun=object. The Review Workflow 1. Turtle (.ttl) Syntax A compact, human readable syntax for writing RDF triples. docs.title: Turtle (.ttl) Syntax
docs.excerpt: A compact, human-readable syntax for writing RDF triples.
docs.text: Turtle (.ttl) Syntax A compact, human readable syntax for writing RDF triples. File extension: .ttl. Uses prefix declarations, semicolons to share subjects, commas to share predicates, and periods to end statement groups. This file is itself written in Turtle. In this section @prefix Declaration Declares a short alias for a namespace IRI. Example: @prefix rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22 rdf syntax ns#> . Prefixes make Turtle readable without them every IRI needs full angle bracket notation. Comma (,) Same Subject and Predicate In Turtle, a comma separates objects that share the same subject and predicate. Example: ex:Earth ex:hasOcean ex:Pacific , ex:Atlantic , ex:Indian . Period (.) End of Statement Group A period terminates a group of triples about the same subject. Semicolon (;) Same Subject In Turtle, a semicolon separates predicate object pairs that share the same subject. Example: ex:Earth rdf:type ex:Planet ; ex:orbits ex:Sun .

docs.title: Software engineering
docs.excerpt: Reckons.AI is built with Reckons.AI, and that is the honest reason this use case is the most detailed one here: it is the only one we have run for a year.
headings: Coding agents that start already knowing
Documentation that cannot quietly go stale
docs.text: Software engineering Reckons.AI is built with Reckons.AI, and that is the honest reason this use case is the most detailed one here: it is the only one we have run for a year. A codebase accumulates decisions faster than anything else you own — why a boundary exists, what a change would break, which claim a test actually pins — and almost none of it survives in the code. It ends up in commit messages nobody re reads, in chat histories that expire, and in the heads of whoever was there. The graph is where those decisions are kept as facts you can query, and the pages you are reading are generated from it. At a glance Audience Anyone maintaining a codebase with more history than any one person remembers — and anyone whose coding agents keep asking questions the last session already answered. Why it is this way Principle The plan lives in the graph, not in the code. A feature exists as an entity with a status before it exists as a file, and the status ladder is honest — speculative, planned, scaffolded, functional, production. A feature is not functional because we wish it were. That single rule is what makes the graph usable as a plan rather than as marketing: you can ask what is actually built and get an answer that has been kept true. Honest Note The gaps are in here too, which is the point of writing them down. On 2026 09 08 a check found that 62% of the generated documentation pages were under 120 words — a title and a paragraph — because thin concepts with no parent cannot be folded into anything. That finding is a fact in this graph, it is why this page is written as a parent with folded children, and you are reading the fix. What we found Measured DOGFOODED AT A REAL SIZE, as of 2026 09 08: seven graphs describing the product, roughly 16,300 facts, with the codebase graph carrying a file link for every git tracked source file. Six alignment gates run on every change and fail the build when the published site stops saying what the graph says. In this section Coding agents that start already knowing An agent queries the same graph over MCP instead of re reading the repository, so the conventions it follows are the ones written down rather than the ones it inferred. Decisions that keep their evidence A benchmark result stays attached to the decision it justified, so next year the question is what the number was, not what someone remembers concluding. Documentation that cannot quietly go stale Pages are generated from the graph, so a page cannot disagree with the facts it was made from without a gate failing. Change the graph and the page follows; hand edit the page and the build tells you. The codebase, as facts Modules, files and their dependencies become entities, so what a change touches is a query rather than a guess. The graph holds the part the source cannot: why the boundary is there. Why a graph, and not a notepad Take one sentence from a real working note: Vantage Suite was dropped at this stage on file format grounds. Related What Is Reckons.AI

docs.title: Why a graph, and not a notepad
docs.excerpt: Take one sentence from a real working note: Vantage Suite was dropped at this stage on file format grounds.
docs.text: Why a graph, and not a notepad Take one sentence from a real working note: Vantage Suite was dropped at this stage on file format grounds. A notepad keeps the sentence. Reckons.AI keeps the fact underneath it. The difference does not show at ten notes and decides everything at a thousand, because the question you will eventually ask is not what did I write, it is what did we drop, and why. The same sentence, two destinations. The divergence is invisible until you ask a question that spans more notes than you can re read. Why it is this way Principle The step in the middle is where you stay in charge. Extraction proposes; nothing enters your graph until you accept it. That is the same review queue the machine's own findings go through, which is why a wrong reading is a thing you correct in one place rather than a wrong sentence you have to remember not to trust. This is not an argument against note taking, and reading it that way loses what it says. Capture should be as close to frictionless as it can be — talking at your phone should be enough. The claim is about what happens AFTER capture: a pile of prose is a pile you must re read, and re reading does not scale. Structure is the price of being able to ask the pile a question later. Honest Note The product has not been showing this. A careful first time reader read Reckons.AI as generic storyboarding and note taking, twice, on 2026 09 06 and again on 2026 09 08 after further exposure. That is a finding about this product rather than about the reader: if the condensation is not visible on the way in, what is left genuinely does look like a notes app that asks you to do extra work in the middle. This page exists because the argument was being asserted and never shown. What we found Measured The divergence is measured, NOT ASSERTED. On 2026 09 08 six local models each read the same short document five times. Twelve relations came back under FIFTY ONE different names. The single relation dropped because was written eleven ways in thirty readings: was eliminated, was dropped on, dropped from shortlist, excluded from shortlist due to, was dropped due to, was dropped from shortlist due to, was eliminated from shortlist, was excluded from shortlist because of, was dropped from shortlist reason, was dropped from shortlist reason for, and dropped from shortlist due to. is a drew eleven names, lacks eight, concern and role five each. Example And the second thing a notepad cannot do: tell you that two of your notes disagree. When a new source arrives, Reckons.AI does not show you everything it found — it shows you what changed: facts that are new, facts that contradict something you already confirmed, and near duplicates of things you already have. The contradictions are the valuable part. A second source disagreeing with the first is the exact moment you want to be interrupted, and it is precisely the moment a folder of documents stays silent — both notes are still there, both still look true, and nothing in the pile knows they cannot both be. That comparison is only possible because the unit is a claim rather than a paragraph. Two paragraphs about the same vendor do not contradict each other in any way a machine can see; two triples with the same subject and predicate and different objects do, exactly and cheaply. It is the same property that makes the fifty one names above a solvable problem instead of a search problem. What that costs you, CONCRETELY. Those eleven phrasings are what a year of your own notes looks like, because you do not phrase things the same way twice either. In a notepad they are eleven unrelated strings: searching dropped finds four of them, and nothing tells you the other seven exist. In a graph they are one relation carrying ten alternative labels, so the question is answered once and completely. That is the whole of the efficiency claim, and it is why the extra step in the middle is not busywork. Example In 'Vantage Suite was dropped on file format grounds': vantage suite = subject, dropped because = predicate, file format = object. Related Watch the diff, not the fact list

headings: Feed it what you are already reading
docs.text: Building a graph for research Functional — built and working, with rough edges still being smoothed. You are investigating something over weeks — a technology choice, a literature area, a decision with real money behind it — and you want what you learn to accumulate instead of scattering across tabs and notes. Research is a loop, not a line. The unanswered questions feed back and direct the next source. At a glance Audience Researcher, analyst, or anyone doing sustained investigation. The primary user this product is for. Starts With An empty graph and a question you cannot yet answer. Ends With A graph where the claims are separable, sourced, and disagreements are visible instead of averaged away. Requests are routed into tasks before the model sees them, and a dictated task lands with no permissions and no acceptance test — so speech is never a route to unsupervised action. docs.text: Comparing your graph to another's Functional — built and working, with rough edges still being smoothed. Two people investigated the same subject and reached different graphs. The interesting output is not the overlap — it is what one holds that the other does not, and the places where both hold a claim and the claims conflict. Their graph is never merged into yours. Disagreement stays legible instead of being averaged away. At a glance Audience Collaborators, reviewers, a team checking its own consensus, or a learner checking their understanding against an expert's graph. Starts With Your graph, and someone else's exported graph file. Ends With A list of genuine disagreements, separated from mere differences of wording. Why it is this way Honest Note The hard part is telling A Real disagreement from A NAMING ONE, and that is not fully solved. Two graphs can say the same thing in different words and look like a conflict, or use one word for two things and look like agreement. Predicate matching by embedding was benchmarked across five models and does not separate synonyms reliably (16.7% caught, negative separation), so wording differences are surfaced for a human rather than resolved automatically. Steps Bring the other graph in as its own graph Import their export as a SEPARATE graph rather than merging it into yours. Merging first destroys the very thing you wanted to see: whose graph said what. Detail Page /kb Read the summary before the rows The diff summary says what KIND of difference you are looking at — mostly additions, mostly conflicts, mostly rewording — so you know whether you are catching up on their research or arguing with it. Detail Page /compare Take what you agree with, keep the rest visible Accepting their fact does not erase yours. A conflict that stays recorded as a conflict is more useful than a resolution nobody can audit later — especially when the two of you turn out to have been reading different sources. Every extracted fact arrives PENDING and stays there until a person confirms it. That single rule is the difference between a graph you can rely on and a transcript of what a language model guessed. Review happens twice, and that is not an accident. Settling the first batch before adding the second is what lets the second batch be matched against something. A graph reviewed only at the end is a pile of claims that never got the chance to connect. headings: Write it the way you would have anyway
docs.text: Keeping everyday notes Scaffolded — the structure exists, but it is incomplete. Expect gaps. You want to write things down the way you always have — loosely, in your own words, without deciding up front what any of it means. The difference here is what happens next: the note is kept as you wrote it AND read for the separate claims inside it, so later you can ask what you actually know rather than search for a paragraph you half remember. The note survives as written; the claims inside it become separately reviewable. The dotted line is the promise that structuring never costs you the original. At a glance Audience Anyone who takes notes. The most common way in, and the least well served today. Starts With A thought, in your own words, with no structure imposed on it. Ends With The note kept verbatim, plus the claims inside it settled as facts you can query and connect. Why it is this way Principle The prose is never the loser. Whatever the extractor makes of a note, the note itself is kept verbatim — fillers, comma splices and all. A system that replaced your sentence with its own reading of it would be asking you to trust a summary of your own thought. Triples stay the core, and freeform is the way in, not an alternative to them. Storing prose and calling it done is the easy version and it forfeits everything downstream: you cannot diff a paragraph, cite half of it, notice it contradicts another one, or record that it left a question open. Freeform capture is worth supporting because typing triples by hand is a terrible way to think — not because the triple was the problem. Honest Note Read the status. You can write a freeform note today at /ingest and it will be extracted into reviewable facts — that part works. What does not exist is a note taking SURFACE: no notebook, no daily page, no editing a note after you wrote it, no browsing your notes as notes rather than as graph nodes. Today a note is an input to extraction and then it is a source record. If you arrived wanting somewhere to keep your thinking, that place is not built yet. What is not done Open Question What is the unit a person sees — the note, or the claims taken out of it? The review queue chose the claim and became unusable at scale; the answer for everyday notes may be the opposite, with claims folded underneath the sentence that produced them. Steps Write it the way you would have anyway No template, no fields, no deciding what kind of note this is. Structure is something the app proposes afterwards, and something you approve — never a form you fill in before you are allowed to write. Reckoning reads the graph as SITUATION (where things stand), TARGET (where you want to be) and PROPOSAL (what would close the gap) — grounded in the facts you confirmed, not in what a model recalls about the subject. A reckoning cites the facts it used, so any part of it can be followed back and disagreed with. At a glance Audience Anyone at the point where research has to become a decision. Starts With A graph with enough confirmed facts to reason over, and a target you can state. Ends With A proposal you can trace back to the specific facts it rests on. Reckoning reasons over the graph, so a graph full of unreviewed pending facts produces a confident proposal resting on claims nobody checked. Run it after a review pass, not instead of one. It states which facts it used, so a proposal you distrust can be traced rather than argued with. 'Choose a platform by Friday' works; 'improve our tooling' does not. Detail Page /reckoning Read the proposal against its evidence Follow the facts the proposal cites back into the graph. Someone who knows a subject has arranged a graph into an ordered walk; you follow it, and the layout changes underneath you as the kind of question changes. A story is a route through a graph, not a slideshow. It ends on an absence deliberately. At a glance Audience Learners, students, anyone handed a graph by an expert. The receiving half of the sharing story. Starts With A graph someone else built, and no obligation to edit it. Ends With Having understood a subject through its structure rather than through prose about it. Why it is this way Honest Note Stories are authored by hand today. There is no story editor: the steps are written as triples in the graph file. That is fine for a starter graph shipped with the app and a real barrier for a teacher who wants to build one for their class. What we found Example static/starter turtles.ttl — kb:turtle story, seven steps across six layouts. Each step asks a question the current view cannot answer, then switches to the layout that can, so layouts arrive as answers rather than as features.
